title: Baron of Aberdeen: every sin mortal of itself; in the regenerate some mortal, some venial
source_text: XXXIV. His affinia sunt quae prolixe & accurate tradit circa distinctionem peccati in mortale & veniale Rob. Baronius ante aliquot annos in Academia Abredonensi apud Scotos Theologiae Professor, Disputatione Theologica de vero discrimine peccati mor-talis & venialis. Ibi enim cum reliquis Reformatis asserit omne peccatum ex se mor-tale esse, nec ullum peccatum esse veniale nisi per accidens: ac praeterea omnia peccata reproborum mortalia esse & dici debere; tum quod mortem aeternam natura sua mereantur, tum quod in illis actu morte aeterna puniantur. Sed pertendit tamen in fidelibus & renatis peccata quaedam mortalia, alia vero venialia summa cum ratione dici. Et mortalia quidem peccata graviora & atrociora in quae fideles ipsi aliquando labuntur. Venialia vero peccata leviora in quae quotidie incurrunt: quia Deus ob illa iram & indi-gnationem iis denunciat, imo exclusionem e coelis mortemque aeternam ipsis intermi-natur: ob haec vero condemnationis aut mortis aeternae metum iis non incutit; imo nec sensum favoris sui, aut fiduciam de remissione peccatorum ab iis aufert.
pass_a_gloss: These things are akin to what Robert Baron, Theology Professor among the Scots in the Academy of Aberdeen some years ago, treats at length and carefully concerning the distinction of sin into mortal and venial, in the Theological Disputation on the true discrimination of mortal and venial sin. For there, with the rest of the Reformed, he asserts that every sin is of itself mortal, and that no sin is venial except by accident: and further that all sins of the reprobate ought to be and to be called mortal—both because by their nature they merit eternal death, and because in them they are actually punished with eternal death. Yet he contends that in the faithful and regenerate certain sins are with highest reason called mortal, others venial. And mortal indeed the heavier and more atrocious sins into which the faithful themselves sometimes fall. Venial however the lighter sins into which they daily run: because for those God denounces wrath and indignation upon them, nay even threatens exclusion from heaven and eternal death; but for these he does not strike them with fear of condemnation or eternal death; nay he does not even take from them the sense of his favor, or confidence concerning the remission of sins.
pass_b_english: Baron’s Aberdeen disputation joins Reformed consent: every sin is mortal of itself; none venial except by accident.
Yet in the regenerate he still distinguishes heavier falls that threaten wrath from daily lighter faults that leave favor and pardon-confidence intact.

choices.why: Baron’s Reformed axiom against intrinsic veniality.
